newsitem.title: UK: Heart attacks bring real fear of flying.
newsitem.headline: Heart attacks bring real fear of flying.

text.p: More airline passengers are dying from heart attacks and other medical emergencies than in plane crashes, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
The latest figures from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration suggest that the number of in-flight medical emergencies has soared in the past decade.
The FAA's data show that there are 14,000 medical emergencies each year on the nine major U.S. airlines, which carry 65 percent of all passengers flown by American carriers.

Applied across all airlines in the United States, this is equivalent to 15 emergencies a day, which compares to the two or three medical emergencies daily found in the last FAA study, between 1986 and 1988.
While each airline has its own definition of a medical emergency, most cases refer to difficulties requiring a request for help from passengers with medical expertise.
Overall, about 350 passengers a year die on board planes operated by U.S. carriers, while an average of 118 passengers a year have died in air crashes on U.S. soil since 1978.

No-one knows why the in-flight death rate has risen, but there are several theories. Most of the deaths occur on long-haul flights, and the number of passengers taking these has doubled in the past decade.

Additionally, more elderly people are flying now and some doctors speculate that the exertion of carrying heavy baggage before a flight and the excitement of holiday travel may increase the risk of heart failure.
